title: Film: Terms and Techniques
description: For beginning film viewers and makers: 100 terms for framing, camera movement, editing, lighting, sound and production, each with a plain-language definition and a practical example.

sources.name: Yale Film Analysis Guide
sources.license: Public educational reference; original definitions and examples

cards.back: A continuous recorded or presented view between edits; on set, the term can also refer to a planned camera setup.
cards.example: A face remains on screen for ten seconds before a cut.

cards.back: One recorded attempt at performing and filming a shot or scene.
cards.example: The director chooses the third take of the doorway entrance.

cards.back: A dramatic unit typically organized around a continuous time and location, though conventions vary.
cards.example: A conversation in a cafe forms one scene.

cards.back: A group of related shots or scenes forming a larger dramatic unit.
cards.example: An escape sequence moves from a prison cell to a road chase.

cards.back: One still image in moving-image media, or the boundaries of the visible image.
cards.example: A doorway is placed near the right edge of the frame.

cards.back: The number of images recorded or displayed per second.
cards.example: A project is displayed at 24 frames per second.

cards.back: The ratio of image width to image height.
cards.example: A 16:9 image is wider than a 4:3 image of the same height.

cards.back: The image's pixel dimensions or its ability to resolve detail, depending on context.
cards.example: A 1920 by 1080 raster has 1920 pixels across.

cards.back: A shot that introduces the setting or spatial context for the following action.
cards.example: A wide view of a school precedes a classroom scene.

cards.back: A framing that emphasizes a large environment, often making people appear very small.
cards.example: A lone rider crosses a vast desert.

cards.back: A framing that shows a subject with substantial surrounding space, often including the whole body.
cards.example: Two people and the room around them are visible.

cards.back: A framing that shows a subject at an intermediate distance, often around the waist upward for a person.
cards.example: A speaker's face and hand gestures share the frame.

cards.back: A tight framing that emphasizes a face or a small subject detail.
cards.example: A worried face fills most of the image.

cards.back: A very tight framing of a small part of a subject.
cards.example: Only an eye and its surrounding skin are visible.

cards.back: A shot containing two principal subjects in the same composition.
cards.example: Both people in a conversation appear together.

cards.back: A view past one person's shoulder toward another subject.
cards.example: A detective is framed beyond a witness's shoulder.

cards.back: A shot representing what a character sees from an approximate viewing position.
cards.example: The audience sees a hallway as the searching character sees it.

cards.back: A closer view of a detail important to the action.
cards.example: A hand turns a key in a lock.

cards.back: A shot of related material outside the main action, often used within an ongoing scene.
cards.example: During a speech, the film cuts to an audience member.

cards.back: A shot emphasizing a character's response to something.
cards.example: A listener silently reacts to unexpected news.

cards.back: A shot covering the main action of a scene broadly enough to establish its overall staging.
cards.example: A full conversation is filmed from one wide setup.

cards.back: Additional camera views that give the editor options for constructing a scene.
cards.example: The crew records close-ups after shooting the master.

cards.back: A shot looking downward at the subject from above.
cards.example: The camera looks down at a person seated on the floor.

cards.back: A shot looking upward at the subject from below.
cards.example: A building is photographed from near ground level.

cards.back: A shot positioned approximately at the subject's eye height.
cards.example: Two seated characters are filmed at their seated eye line.

cards.back: A shot with the camera tilted around its viewing axis so the horizon appears slanted.
cards.example: A corridor's vertical lines lean diagonally in the image.

cards.back: A view from high above, often looking nearly straight down.
cards.example: A crowd forms patterns when seen from overhead.

cards.back: Rotation of the camera left or right around a fixed position.
cards.example: The camera turns to follow a walking actor.

cards.back: Rotation of the camera upward or downward around a fixed position.
cards.example: The view rises from a person's shoes to their face.

cards.back: A shot in which the camera physically travels on a wheeled support or equivalent moving platform.
cards.example: The camera moves toward a doorway rather than zooming.

cards.back: A shot in which the camera moves through space, often following a subject.
cards.example: The camera travels beside a running character.

cards.back: A lateral camera move to the left or right, often on a dolly.
cards.example: The camera slides sideways to reveal a second person.

cards.back: A shot made with the camera on a crane or similar arm, enabling sweeping changes in height and position.
cards.example: The camera rises above a crowd to reveal a courtyard.

cards.back: A shot made while the operator holds and supports the camera, often retaining some bodily movement.
cards.example: Small shakes accompany a character running upstairs.

cards.back: A stabilizing support that allows camera orientation to remain controlled during movement.
cards.example: An operator walks while the camera stays relatively level.

cards.back: A change in lens focal length that alters framing without moving the camera position.
cards.example: A distant sign grows larger while perspective remains fixed.

cards.back: A combined camera move and opposite zoom adjustment that changes background perspective while keeping the subject roughly the same size.
cards.example: A character remains large while the hallway seems to stretch.

cards.back: A visible shift of focus from one subject or distance to another within a shot.
cards.example: Focus moves from a foreground glass to a person behind it.

cards.back: The range of distances that appear acceptably sharp in an image.
cards.example: A portrait has a sharp face and a blurred background.

cards.back: Use of a narrow depth of field to isolate a limited distance range.
cards.example: A nearby hand is sharp while the room is soft.

cards.back: An approach in which foreground and background subjects remain acceptably sharp.
cards.example: Both a child near the camera and a doorway far away are clear.

cards.back: A lens property that, with image-sensor size, helps determine angle of view and magnification.
cards.example: A shorter focal length gives a wider view on the same sensor.

cards.back: A lens giving a relatively broad angle of view for the imaging format.
cards.example: A small room can be shown from a close camera position.

cards.back: In common film usage, a lens with a relatively narrow angle of view that magnifies distant subjects.
cards.example: A distant actor is framed tightly from across a street.

cards.back: The lens opening that controls how much light passes through; it also influences depth of field.
cards.example: Opening the aperture admits more light and can blur the background.

cards.back: The amount of light recorded by the imaging medium, controlled by settings and illumination.
cards.example: A brighter exposure reveals more detail in a dim room.

cards.back: The duration each frame is exposed, affecting motion blur as well as light capture.
cards.example: A short exposure makes fast-moving droplets look crisp.

cards.back: Adjustment of color response so a chosen neutral reference appears neutral under the lighting.
cards.example: A white card is used to reduce an unwanted blue cast.

cards.back: The arrangement of visible elements in a scene, including sets, performers, props, costume and lighting.
cards.example: A cramped set and crowded props emphasize confinement.

cards.back: Planned positions and movements of performers within a scene.
cards.example: An actor crosses to the window after delivering a line.

cards.back: The arrangement of visual elements within the frame.
cards.example: A subject is balanced against an open doorway.

cards.back: A composition guideline that places important elements near lines dividing the image into thirds or their intersections.
cards.example: A face sits near the upper-right intersection.

cards.back: The space between a subject's head and the top of the frame.
cards.example: The camera reframes to reduce empty space above the actor.

cards.back: Space in front of a subject's direction of movement or gaze.
cards.example: A walking person has open space ahead of them.

cards.back: The direction in which a performer appears to look.
cards.example: The actor looks just beside the lens toward an imagined partner.

cards.back: The apparent direction of movement or orientation within the image.
cards.example: A car continues moving left to right across consecutive shots.

cards.back: A continuity guideline that keeps cameras on one side of an action axis to preserve screen relationships.
cards.example: Opposing speakers keep consistent left-right positions.

cards.back: A guideline recommending a substantial camera-angle change between similar views to avoid a jarring near-match.
cards.example: The second setup moves well around the actor rather than only slightly.

cards.back: Editing that emphasizes clear spatial and temporal relationships so the action feels coherent.
cards.example: Matched looks and movements make separate setups feel continuous.

cards.back: A cut that joins views of the same action at compatible points in its movement.
cards.example: A hand begins opening a door in one shot and finishes in another.

cards.back: A cut connecting a character's look with a shot of what the character is understood to see.
cards.example: A glance upward is followed by a ceiling light.

cards.back: Alternation between opposing views, often of conversational partners.
cards.example: The editor alternates each speaker's close-up.

cards.back: An immediate transition from one shot to another.
cards.example: A room view instantly changes to a face.

cards.back: A discontinuous cut between similar views that makes time or action appear to jump.
cards.example: A seated speaker abruptly changes posture in the same framing.

cards.back: A cut linking shots through a visual, movement or conceptual similarity.
cards.example: A round clock face cuts to a similarly framed moon.

cards.back: Alternating between separate actions or locations, often implying simultaneity or a narrative relationship.
cards.example: A rescue team and a trapped person appear in alternating shots.

cards.back: An arrangement of shots that creates meaning through their combination; often a sequence that compresses time.
cards.example: Brief practice scenes show an athlete improving over weeks.

cards.back: Omission of part of an action or period of story time.
cards.example: A traveler packs, and the next shot shows their arrival.

cards.back: A transition in which one image gradually fades out while another fades in.
cards.example: A daytime landscape blends into the same location at night.

cards.back: A gradual transition from an image to a uniform field, commonly black.
cards.example: The final image slowly disappears into black.

cards.back: A gradual transition from a uniform field, commonly black, to an image.
cards.example: A dark screen slowly reveals a bedroom.

cards.back: A transition in which a moving boundary replaces one image with another.
cards.example: A line travels across the screen, revealing the next scene.

cards.back: A shot of unusually long uninterrupted duration in its context.
cards.example: A conversation plays for several minutes without a cut.

cards.back: An effect in which movement is shown more slowly than it occurred, often by recording at a higher frame rate than playback.
cards.example: A leap appears to last several seconds.

cards.back: An effect created by capturing images at intervals and playing them back faster than the events unfolded.
cards.example: Clouds race across the sky over a few seconds.

cards.back: An image held still instead of continuing normal motion.
cards.example: A runner's midair pose remains on screen.

cards.back: Sound belonging to the film's story world, whether its source is on screen or off screen.
cards.example: Music comes from a radio in the scene.

cards.back: Sound presented outside the story world's immediate sound environment.
cards.example: An orchestral score accompanies a silent landscape.

cards.back: Performed and recorded sound effects synchronized to actions in the picture.
cards.example: A performer records footsteps to match an actor's walk.

cards.back: Automated dialogue replacement: rerecording dialogue after filming to replace or supplement production dialogue.
cards.example: An actor rerecords a line obscured by wind during filming.

cards.back: The background sound of a location recorded without intentional dialogue or action.
cards.example: Quiet room ambience fills gaps between dialogue edits.

cards.back: Environmental background sound that establishes a setting.
cards.example: Traffic and distant voices suggest a busy street.

cards.back: Sound that connects shots or scenes across a visual transition.
cards.example: Train noise begins before the image cuts to a station.

cards.back: An edit in which the incoming scene's audio begins before its image appears.
cards.example: We hear the next speaker while still seeing the listener.
cards.hint: Think about which arrives first: incoming sound or incoming image.

cards.back: An edit in which the outgoing scene's audio continues after the image changes.
cards.example: A departing character's words continue over the next image.

cards.back: A voice heard over images without the speaker visibly delivering those words in that moment; it may be narration or another form of off-image speech.
cards.example: An older narrator describes a childhood memory.

cards.back: Balancing and combining dialogue, effects, ambience and music into the final soundtrack.
cards.example: Music is lowered so a quiet line remains audible.

cards.back: The principal light shaping a subject's appearance in a lighting setup.
cards.example: A lamp to one side provides the face's dominant illumination.

cards.back: Light used to reduce contrast by brightening areas shadowed by the key light.
cards.example: A reflector softens the dark side of a face.

cards.back: Light coming from behind a subject, often helping separate it from the background.
cards.example: A rim of light outlines a person's hair.

cards.back: A common setup using key, fill and backlight with distinct roles.
cards.example: The face is shaped by a key, softened by fill and separated by backlight.

cards.back: A relatively bright, low-contrast lighting style with limited deep shadows.
cards.example: A cheerful studio scene has evenly lit faces and surroundings.

cards.back: A lighting style emphasizing contrast and substantial shadow areas.
cards.example: A small pool of light reveals only part of a face.

cards.back: A light source visible within the scene, such as a lamp or candle.
cards.example: A bedside lamp appears in frame and contributes to the lighting.

cards.back: Lighting designed to seem justified by a believable source in the scene.
cards.example: An off-camera fixture imitates light entering through a window.

cards.back: Creative adjustment of image color and tonal relationships to establish a look and maintain visual coherence.
cards.example: Cooler shadows give a night scene a consistent mood.

cards.back: A sequence of drawings showing planned shots or visual action.
cards.example: Panels map out the camera views for a chase.

cards.back: A written plan of shots to capture, often including framing, action and technical notes.
cards.example: The crew checks off wide views and close-ups during filming.

cards.back: Supplementary footage used to support primary action, narration or interviews.
cards.example: Shots of machinery accompany an interview with an engineer.

cards.back: A colored backdrop used for chroma-key compositing to replace the background.
cards.example: A studio performer is composited into a mountain setting.
